newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bullish DAX gains 1.3 percent, sets fresh records.
newsitem.headline: Bullish DAX gains 1.3 percent, sets fresh records.

text.p: A strongly bullish tone reigned on the German stock market on Wednesday, sending the blue chip DAX index to fresh all-time highs.

Spurred on by a global markets boom, Tuesday's benign U.S. consumer prices report and the dollar's continued rally, the DAX gained 39.57 points, or 1.3 percent, to end the floor session at 2,988.45 -- a record close.

Although the DAX failed to make the magic 3,000-point level which many dealers had said they were aiming for and slipped from an intraday high of 2,997.05, most traders agreed that the near-term outlook was good.
Wednesday's rally mainly extended gains begun in post-bourse trade on Tuesday after a benign U.S. consumer price report eased fears about a U.S. rate hike.
"No matter what, I think the DAX has leeway to rise another 100 points in the next 14 days," said a Munich trader.
"A dollar at this level is going to mean windfall profits for a lot of companies and we will see that reflected in earnings statements at the year end," he added.
Chemical shares and other dollar-sensitive stocks were the stars of the day.

Schering AG rose 1.60 marks to 138.90 marks after its chief financial officer Klaus Pohle told a German newspaper he expected the company to keep increasing its dividends in coming years so long as profits kept rising.
BASF AG ended up 1.74 marks at 60.59, despite denying a press report that its dividend payout would exceed one billion marks for 1996 which had triggered initial gains in its shares.

Airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG was up 69 pfennigs at 21.70 marks, repairing some of its losses from Tuesday over a new draft law that would eventually limit foreign ownership of its stock. Analysts said that drop was exaggerated.
Not all observers were confident that the current bull market would last.

Commerzbank equity strategist Thomas Tilse told Reuters Financial Television: "This looks like the best of all worlds for German stocks and we will be testing the 3,000 level. But beyond that the outlook is quite bleak."
By the end of 1997, Tilse predicted the DAX would have dropped to 2,800 points.
"Company earnings for 1997 are already priced into the market and I think realism will prevail for most of 1997."
